original_question: Develop a limit-shape theory for Young-Fibonacci diagrams by defining an appropriate scaling between diagram sizes, for example through a nearly isometric doubling embedding D: YF_r(k) -> YF_r(2k), and then determine whether randomly chosen r-colored permutations admit a limit shape in the resulting limit space and, if so, identify that limit shape.
target_in_paper: Section 2 (Problems of 2025), Problem 7. More precisely, your draft is targeting the official problem: develop a limit-shape theory for Young–Fibonacci diagrams by first defining a scaling between ranks, for example via a doubling embedding D: YF_r^(k) -> YF_r^(2k), and then ask whether the Young–Fibonacci diagrams arising from randomly chosen r-colored permutations have a limit shape in the resulting limit space. Problem 5 supplies the notebook’s intended model of what a 'limit-shape theory' should mean, while Problems 9 and 17 clarify the tableau/lattice language and the notation YF_r.
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper’s actual target. It correctly identifies that the problem is about Young–Fibonacci diagrams rather than ordinary Young diagrams, that the first obstacle is to define an asymptotically meaningful scaling between ranks, that a doubling map D: YF_r^(k) -> YF_r^(2k) is the paper’s concrete example, and that the end goal is to decide whether diagrams coming from random r-colored permutations have a limit shape and to determine it if it exists.
missing_details: The exact target is Problem 7, framed as developing a 'similar theory of limit shapes' parallel to the ordinary Young-diagram theory described immediately beforehand in Problem 5.
The paper does not simply ask for any scaling: in the doubling example, the map D must be 'nearly isometric' with respect to the Hasse-diagram distance on YF_r.

The paper’s 'nearly isometric' requirement has three parts that should all be stated: nearby words should map to nearby words, conversely nearby images should come from nearby preimages, and every word in YF_r should be near some point of the image of D.
The notation YF_r^(k) should be explained as the rank-k words/diagrams in the r-differential Young–Fibonacci lattice YF_r.
The paper explicitly says that the scaling map is meant to define a limit space first; only inside that limit space is the limit-shape question posed.

The draft omits the paper’s restriction that, because YF_r as a dual graded graph has unique weighting 1, there are no tableau colorings and only three natural distributions of diagrams are to be considered.
If one wants the question to be stand-alone, it helps to note that Young–Fibonacci tableaux are identified in the paper with upward paths in the Young–Fibonacci lattice.

Problem 5 supplies the notebook’s intended meaning of 'limit shape' by analogy, namely an asymptotic deterministic shape after rescaling as size tends to infinity; Problem 7 itself leaves that notion implicit until the scaling/limit space is chosen.
refined_question: Let YF_r be the r-differential Young–Fibonacci lattice, and let YF_r^(k) denote its rank-k words (diagrams). Develop, in the sense of the ordinary Young-diagram limit-shape theory recalled in Problem 5, a limit-shape theory for YF_r by first defining a scaling between ranks—e.g. a doubling embedding D: YF_r^(k) -> YF_r^(2k) that is nearly isometric for the Hasse-diagram metric, meaning that it sends nearby words to nearby words, reflects nearness back to preimages, and has image coarsely dense in YF_r. In the resulting limit space, as n -> infinity, do the Young–Fibonacci diagrams associated with random r-colored permutations of size n admit a deterministic limit shape, under the three natural diagram distributions available because YF_r has unique weighting 1 as a dual graded graph? If so, determine that limit shape.
justification: The draft is plainly aimed at Problem 7: it mentions Young–Fibonacci diagrams, the need for a scaling between sizes, the sample doubling map D: YF_r^(k) -> YF_r^(2k), and the final question about random r-colored permutations and a limit shape, all of which appear in the official wording of Problem 7. To make the question paper-faithful and stand-alone, the refined version restores the exact Hasse-metric 'nearly isometric' conditions that Problem 7 imposes on D, makes explicit that the scaling is used to build a limit space before the limit-shape question is even well-posed, and adds the restriction to the three natural diagram distributions forced by the unique weighting 1 of YF_r. Problem 5 is the nearby context that explains what 'a similar theory of limit shapes' means in this notebook, while Problems 9 and 17 clarify the tableau/upward-path language and identify YF_r as the r-differential Young–Fibonacci lattice.
